title: Mixed-workload scheduler prototype - results review + rollout plan (runtime/SRE/perf)
topics: Prototype benchmark readout (mixed prompt distributions, trace replay)
Backpressure and admission control by class
Canary plan: perf-canary A/B + limited production slice
summary: Cross-team review of mixed-workload scheduler prototype results and readiness for a guarded rollout. Perf showed meaningful p95 improvements for short/interactive requests in mixed distributions with a small throughput dip in one scenario; one p95 regression case was linked to misclassification and a priority inversion edge where long-prefill batching blocked short requests. Team aligned on keeping the feature flag default-off in runtime-1.19, running perf-canary A/B with starvation/queue-depth alerting, then enabling for a very small Dedicated slice with explicit rollback triggers (queue depth growth, starvation signals, p95/p99 regressions beyond agreed bounds). Action items captured for benchmark reruns, fairness simulation gate, dashboard/alert finalization, and release notes/operator guidance.
action_items: Rina Kobayashi - Re-run trace replay suite with classifier EWMA enabled and attach side-by-side tables (p50/p95/p99 + throughput + GPU util) - due 2024-11-25
Sana Farid - Define final go/no-go criteria for canary readout template (what graphs, what deltas) and share with SRE + perf - due 2024-11-26
Aisha Bello - Finalize starvation + backlog alerts (thresholds + paging vs ticketing) and update the dashboard spec - due 2024-11-27
Peter Holtz - Validate overload behavior with separate admission thresholds per class (short vs long) under burst; document recommended defaults - due 2024-11-27
Sahana Iyer - Add CI gate for fairness simulation test harness (max-wait bound + long-queue service share) and wire into runtime perf pipeline - due 2024-11-29
Connor O'Brien - Confirm runtime-1.19 release train landing plan: flag default-off, config surface names, and rollback steps - due 2024-11-26
Omar El-Sayed - Publish metric naming map (final names for queue depth, wait histograms, starvation indicator) for dashboards + on-call - due 2024-11-26
next_steps: Complete benchmark reruns with updated classifier safeguards; verify the previously regressing scenario is neutral or improved.
Enable perf-canary A/B (baseline vs flag on) and monitor queue depth, wait histograms, and starvation indicators for 48–72 hours.
If perf-canary is green, proceed to limited production slice on Dedicated (single region, small percentage) with staffed on-call and explicit rollback triggers.
Write canary readout with recommendation and link to evidence artifacts (tables, dashboard snapshots, diff notes).
Decision meeting to determine whether to keep as opt-in for specific tiers/routes or continue iteration before broader rollout.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Mixed-workload scheduler prototype - results review + rollout plan (runtime/SRE/perf)
Date: 2024-11-21 17:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Talia Benson, Sofia Ivanova, Omar El-Sayed, Jonas Weber, Rina Kobayashi, Sana Farid, Sean Gallagher, Rafael Mendes, Aisha Bello, Tomáš Novák, Peter Holtz, Sahana Iyer, Connor O'Brien, Benji Okafor

---

[00:00] Talia Benson: Okay, hi everyone. Thanks for jumping. Goal today is, um, quick readout on prototype results, risks we still believe are real, and align on rollout steps. We need to be crisp because release train for 1.19 is looming.

[00:22] Sofia Ivanova: Yep. And we’ll keep it focused on what we can safely ship behind the flag.

[00:28] Jonas Weber: I’m recording notes from perf side. We’ve got the latest mixed workload runs from Rina’s harness, plus the canary infra PR is almost done.

[00:37] Sean Gallagher: From SRE perspective, I want to come out with clear rollback triggers. Like, not vibes. A number.

[00:45] Talia Benson: Great. Sofia, do you want to start with the top line deltas?

[00:50] Sofia Ivanova: Sure. So: two-queue policy with short-first plus fairness window, plus the guardrails for max-wait and periodic long service. Under the mixed prompt distributions we defined—so like 70/30 short/long, and then 50/50—short request p95 improved materially versus FIFO. Numbers vary by model and SKU, but we’re seeing on the order of like 18 to 30 percent p95 improvement for the short class.

[01:17] Omar El-Sayed: And p99 got less spiky. That was the main thing—tail smoothing. The average didn’t move much.

[01:23] Sofia Ivanova: Right. But there is a cost: we saw a throughput dip in one scenario, and we saw a regression case, which I think we can explain and fix.

[01:33] Rina Kobayashi: To be precise, the throughput dip was around 2.5-ish percent on the A100 run with heavy long contexts. It’s not catastrophic but it’s there.

[01:42] Jonas Weber: And the regression was in the “bursty arrivals + long-prefill spikes” scenario. Short p95 actually got worse by like, what, 8 percent? Something like that.

[01:52] Rina Kobayashi: Yeah, it was single-digit but real. It correlates with a classifier mislabeling plus batching behavior. Like the scheduler thought it had short work but it wasn’t.

[02:03] Sean Gallagher: Can you explain “mislabeling” in non-hand-wavy terms? Because this is the thing that bites us in production.

[02:10] Omar El-Sayed: Yeah. Our current classifier is basically prompt length threshold plus a predicted prefill cost stub. In that regression run, we had requests with moderate prompt length but high prefill time because of… basically the kernel path chosen and sequence-length distribution. So they got routed into short queue, then they joined a prefill batch that was actually long-running.

[02:31] Sofia Ivanova: And that caused short queue to not be actually short. So it’s priority inversion by classification error.

[02:38] Tomáš Novák: Sorry, just to sanity check: short requests were blocked behind a long prefill batch. That sounds like the bug that Marcus mentioned in Slack.

[02:46] Sofia Ivanova: Yes. We have a regression test now from that load test. The fix is in the PR that prevents a long prefill batch from holding the dispatch when short queue has work—basically breaking the “sticky” batch formation.

[03:03] Jonas Weber: That was PR 8468, I think. “Priority inversion bug fix.”

[03:06] Sofia Ivanova: Correct.

[03:09] Aisha Bello: Before we get deep: for dashboards, I need final metric names. We can’t keep renaming “queue_wait_seconds” every other day.

[03:17] Omar El-Sayed: Fair. I’ll publish the mapping after this.

[03:22] Talia Benson: Great. Let’s do results, then risks, then rollout. Jonas, can you share the perf readout in words? Assume no one has the sheet open.

[03:32] Jonas Weber: Yep. Across synthetic mixes: short p95 improved 20-ish percent, long p95 got slightly worse in some cases, like 3 to 6 percent, but bounded. Total tokens per second: mostly within noise, except that one heavy-long scenario where it dipped ~2 to 3 percent. GPU util basically unchanged.

[03:54] Jonas Weber: On trace replay—representative customer-ish distribution—short p95 improved more, like 25 to 35 percent, because the baseline is pretty bad when you co-schedule huge summarize jobs with chat.

[04:08] Sean Gallagher: And what about timeouts? Like, do we push long requests into timeout territory?

[04:13] Rina Kobayashi: We didn’t see timeouts in the harness, but our harness uses generous client timeouts. We did look at max wait time and queue depth.

[04:22] Omar El-Sayed: That’s where the starvation indicators come in. We now emit per-class queue depth and wait histograms, and we compute “max observed wait” for long queue, plus a “starvation_guardrail_triggered” counter.

[04:37] Rafael Mendes: I need to understand the reliability angle: if short-first always wins, long queue builds, we get memory blowups or whatever, then the whole thing fails. What prevents that under overload?

[04:50] Peter Holtz: That’s the backpressure work. Separate admission thresholds by class, plus global cap. Under overload, we reject—or rather we shed—long class earlier so short remains within SLO. But it’s configurable.

[05:06] Sean Gallagher: That’s fine but that’s product policy too. Dedicated customers may not be happy if we start shedding summarization.

[05:13] Talia Benson: That’s why it’s behind a flag and targeted rollout. We’re not changing defaults broadly.

[05:20] Sofia Ivanova: Also: fairness window. We guarantee that after N short dispatches we force service from long, regardless of short backlog. That bounds starvation.

[05:32] Sahana Iyer: Just to add: we’re adding simulation-based tests in CI that stress arrival patterns. Like bursty short plus constant long. It verifies long receives at least X percent of service and max wait doesn’t exceed a bound.

[05:49] Sean Gallagher: “Bound” depends on what? Because runtime conditions vary.

[05:54] Sahana Iyer: Bound is configured per test scenario based on synthetic service times. It’s more regression detection than absolute SLO.

[06:04] Sean Gallagher: Okay. I like regression detection. For on-call we still need alerting that is simple.

[06:10] Aisha Bello: For alerting I’m thinking: long queue depth growing for >10 minutes plus starvation trigger count above threshold, ticket. For paging: short p95 regression beyond X percent in canary vs control, plus queue depth anomalies.

[06:27] Rafael Mendes: Paging should be minimal. If this is canary, sure, but I don’t want a million pages.

[06:32] Sana Farid: For canary we can staff it. The goal is to learn quickly; paging is okay if it’s calibrated and time-boxed.

[06:41] Connor O'Brien: Release constraint: runtime-1.19 can include flag plumbing and code path default-off. Ops change is only if someone flips the flag.

[06:51] Benji Okafor: And config system supports it. The flag is scoped by route and tier if we want. We can do “Dedicated only” or even one cluster.

[07:01] Talia Benson: Okay. Let’s enumerate the remaining risks. Sofia, start with misclassification.

[07:08] Sofia Ivanova: Risk one: misclassification. If we classify long as short, we harm the short queue. If we classify short as long, we lose the benefit but it’s safe. So default should be conservative: only call something short if we’re confident.

[07:25] Omar El-Sayed: That’s why we added the EWMA: rolling estimate of observed prefill time per request shape. It’s not perfect, but it corrects some systematic errors.

[07:36] Rina Kobayashi: But EWMA can be noisy on cold start, like after deploy.

[07:41] Omar El-Sayed: Yes. We have a warmup period where we fall back to prompt-length threshold.

[07:48] Jonas Weber: Plus perf-canary runs long enough to get past warmup.

[07:52] Tomáš Novák: Risk two: oscillation? Like if queue flips between short and long and you get jitter.

[07:58] Sofia Ivanova: Yes. Two-queue with fairness window can oscillate under burst. We saw some “sawtooth” in queue depth when bursts align. It’s not severe in the results but we should watch.

[08:12] Peter Holtz: That’s also backpressure. If you let long in at same rate during a short burst, you create backlog. If you cap long admissions during burst, you stabilize.

[08:23] Sean Gallagher: I want to make sure we don’t call it “admission control” in release notes like it’s a new product policy. This is internal control plane behavior.

[08:33] Connor O'Brien: We can phrase it as “separate per-class queue thresholds” or “overload guardrails.”

[08:38] Talia Benson: Okay. Risk three: throughput regression. Jonas, what’s acceptable?

[08:45] Jonas Weber: For the performance standard we proposed: throughput regression should be within 3 percent in mixed workloads, ideally within 1 percent. We can accept a small dip if tail improvement is strong, but we need to be explicit.

[09:01] Sean Gallagher: From SRE: I’m less worried about 2 percent tokens/sec than I am about pathological backlog growth, because that’s where incidents come from.

[09:10] Aisha Bello: Agreed. So we should alert on queue depth slope, not just absolute.

[09:15] Omar El-Sayed: Yep. We can do derivative-ish. At least a “queue depth increasing for N minutes” check.

[09:22] Sana Farid: Another risk: interpretability. If on-call sees p95 shift, they need a breakdown: wait vs service time, prefill vs decode. Otherwise we can’t tell if scheduler helped or if kernel path changed.

[09:38] Omar El-Sayed: We have prefill/decode split metrics and trace spans for enqueue/dequeue. There’s a bit of sampling though.

[09:46] Tomáš Novák: Speaking of sampling, in incidents sampling is always the thing that fails. Can we bump sampling in canary?

[09:52] Omar El-Sayed: We can bump for canary cluster, yes. We’ll keep it limited.

[09:58] Talia Benson: Okay. Let’s go into rollout plan. I’d like to align on the exact stages and who signs off.

[10:06] Sana Farid: My proposal: stage 0 is lab benchmarks complete. stage 1 is perf-canary A/B baseline vs flag on, running same trace replay daily. stage 2 is limited prod slice: single region, small percentage of Dedicated traffic, only for selected routes that are known to be mixed workload heavy.

[10:28] Sean Gallagher: And a stage 2 requires SRE approval with rollback triggers. I want that in writing.

[10:34] Rafael Mendes: For stage 2, we should staff an on-call buddy system, at least first 24 hours.

[10:41] Connor O'Brien: Timing-wise, runtime-1.19 can ship with the flag and metrics. The earliest we can do stage 2 is after we verify perf-canary on that build.

[10:53] Benji Okafor: Also: enablement mechanism. We can do a config override in control plane, no redeploy required.

[11:00] Sofia Ivanova: But we should keep it “default off” and “explicit allowlist.” No broad rollout.

[11:07] Talia Benson: Okay. What are rollback triggers? Let’s hash.

[11:12] Sean Gallagher: I’ll propose:
1) Short p95 increases >10% relative to control for >15 minutes.
2) Long queue starvation signal triggers continuously, or max wait exceeds, say, 2x baseline.
3) Queue depth grows monotonically for >10 minutes beyond a threshold.

[11:34] Aisha Bello: We can implement 1 with A/B comparisons on dashboards, but in prod you don’t always have a control.

[11:41] Sean Gallagher: For stage 2 we can split: canary cluster vs baseline cluster, or route-level split.

[11:47] Benji Okafor: Route-level split is doable but it’s more complex. Cluster-level is easier: one small cluster with flag on.

[11:56] Rafael Mendes: Cluster-level also makes rollback simpler.

[12:01] Jonas Weber: For canary we already have A/B in perf-canary infra: baseline and flag-on runs on same hardware, publishing diffs.

[12:12] Sana Farid: For production stage, we can do one Dedicated cell with scheduler on. Compare to sibling cell in same region.

[12:21] Tomáš Novák: But be careful with traffic differences. We need to ensure same customer? Or else the comparison is noisy.

[12:28] Sofia Ivanova: Ideally we pick a customer with stable traffic and mixed workload pattern, and we split within their dedicated deployment. But that’s product decision.

[12:37] Talia Benson: We’re not naming customers here, but yes, we can coordinate with Dedicated PM offline.

[12:44] Sean Gallagher: Regardless, alerting should not depend on perfect control. We can set absolute thresholds too.

[12:52] Aisha Bello: Okay, absolute triggers:
- short queue depth > X for Y minutes
- short wait p95 > Z ms for Y minutes
- starvation counter > N per minute
We need to pick X, Y, Z, N.

[13:10] Omar El-Sayed: We can set them relative to baseline from the last 24 hours. Like dynamic thresholds.

[13:17] Sean Gallagher: Dynamic thresholds are a footgun.

[13:20] Omar El-Sayed: Fair. Then pick conservative fixed thresholds for canary only.

[13:25] Rafael Mendes: Can we at least use fixed thresholds that are “obviously bad” so it’s not chatty?

[13:32] Aisha Bello: Yes. I’ll propose numbers after reviewing typical queue depths on those routes.

[13:38] Talia Benson: Great. Can we talk about operator-visible changes? Connor, release notes.

[13:44] Connor O'Brien: For runtime-1.19 we’ll note: “Feature flag: mixed-workload scheduler (short/long aware) available for testing; default off.” Also mention new metrics. No API changes.

[13:56] Tomáš Novák: Add “how to disable quickly” in the runbook. Like one command.

[14:01] Benji Okafor: That’s simple: config toggle. We’ll document the exact key.

[14:06] Sofia Ivanova: Also we should note that enabling it changes fairness behavior. Long requests may see slightly higher latency in exchange for short tail improvement.

[14:17] Sean Gallagher: That’s the part that will get escalations if someone flips it without telling people.

[14:22] Sana Farid: Which is why enablement requires approvals.

[14:25] Talia Benson: Let’s define approval chain: stage 1 perf-canary is perf+runtime, stage 2 production canary requires SRE signoff plus runtime lead plus perf.

[14:38] Sean Gallagher: Works.

[14:40] Jonas Weber: Works.

[14:41] Sofia Ivanova: Works.

[14:44] Talia Benson: Back to the regression scenario—do we believe the fix plus classifier EWMA resolves it? Rina?

[14:52] Rina Kobayashi: I haven’t rerun with both changes yet. With just the inversion fix, it improved but not fully. With EWMA alone it helped in a different scenario. So I need a combined run.

[15:06] Sofia Ivanova: That’s a must-have before any prod canary.

[15:09] Sean Gallagher: Agreed.

[15:11] Omar El-Sayed: Also: the instrumentation showed the wait time moved from short to long queue as intended. So the scheduler is doing what it says.

[15:21] Tomáš Novák: What about lock contention? We added per-class queues; any overhead?

[15:27] Sofia Ivanova: There was a small contention increase; Marcus optimized it. It’s in a PR but not sure if merged. It reduced CPU overhead.

[15:36] Jonas Weber: It’s PR 8495. Perf impact was minimal after that.

[15:41] Connor O'Brien: Need to check if it’s in 1.19 cut. If not, we might not want to enable in prod until it is.

[15:50] Talia Benson: Action item: Connor check release inclusion, but let’s keep moving.

[15:56] Peter Holtz: I want to revisit overload. In real bursts, if we only prioritize short without gating long admissions, you get memory pressure and queue growth. Separate thresholds help. But what defaults do we want when flag is on?

[16:12] Sofia Ivanova: We should set safe defaults: slightly lower long admission threshold, keep short high. But I don’t want to accidentally create silent long shedding.

[16:22] Sean Gallagher: For canary, shedding is okay if we understand it and it’s deliberate. For production beyond canary, product needs to sign off.

[16:30] Sana Farid: For canary readout we can explicitly call out any increase in 429s or whatever for long class.

[16:38] Omar El-Sayed: Our backpressure returns are currently “server busy” type errors; we can tag them by class.

[16:46] Aisha Bello: Good. Then I can dashboard “admission rejects by class.”

[16:51] Rafael Mendes: Please make sure it’s not a brand new metric name the day before canary.

[16:56] Omar El-Sayed: Understood.

[16:59] Talia Benson: Let’s talk about which dashboards we’ll use during canary.

[17:04] Aisha Bello: Minimum set:
- per-class queue depth
- per-class wait time p50/p95
- overall route latency p50/p95/p99 with breakdown (queue vs service)
- starvation indicator (counter + max wait)
- throughput tokens/sec and GPU util
- error rates including admission rejects by class

[17:27] Sean Gallagher: And SLO error budget burn. Even if it’s canary, we should watch burn rate.

[17:33] Tomáš Novák: Plus “batch size distribution” if possible. That helps detect the prefill-batch stickiness.

[17:40] Omar El-Sayed: We can surface it. Might be in logs rather than metrics though.

[17:45] Sofia Ivanova: We added sampled structured logs for scheduler decisions. That includes selected queue, fairness window state, and observed wait.

[17:55] Rafael Mendes: Sampled logs are fine. Just make sure they’re discoverable.

[18:00] Sana Farid: For canary I want a single page link. Not 12 Kibana searches.

[18:05] Omar El-Sayed: We’ll link from the dashboard to the log explorer query.

[18:11] Talia Benson: Great. Any open questions before we lock decisions?

[18:16] Jonas Weber: Question: throughput regression bounds. Are we okay with 3%? Or do we require <2% for stage 2?

[18:26] Sean Gallagher: For stage 2, I’d accept up to 3% if short p95 improvement is substantial and no backlog risk. But if we see backlog growth, that’s a no.

[18:37] Sofia Ivanova: Agreed. Throughput is secondary for this prototype; tail is primary.

[18:44] Peter Holtz: But throughput affects cost. If it’s 3% permanent, product will care.

[18:49] Talia Benson: For prototype canary, accept up to 3% as temporary learning, but decision to graduate will require stricter bounds.

[18:58] Sana Farid: I’ll encode that in the go/no-go criteria: “Stage 2 go: short p95 improves >=15% vs baseline; throughput regression <=3%; no starvation; no queue depth growth trend; no new error mode.”

[19:17] Sean Gallagher: Add “no increase in incident-style pages” or “page threshold.”

[19:22] Rafael Mendes: Please don’t create a KPI of pages.

[19:25] (crosstalk)

[19:27] Talia Benson: Okay, let’s keep it objective: no sustained alert firing beyond agreed thresholds.

[19:34] Connor O'Brien: Another question: naming. Is it “mixed workload scheduler” or “short-long scheduler”? We need consistency.

[19:42] Sofia Ivanova: Mixed workload scheduler. The policy is short/long aware.

[19:47] Omar El-Sayed: Metric prefix could be “scheduler_mixed_” to avoid collisions.

[19:51] Aisha Bello: Please don’t change it again.

[19:53] Omar El-Sayed: (laughs) okay.

[20:00] Talia Benson: Okay, moving to closing. Let’s recap decisions and action items.

[20:06] Talia Benson: Decision 1: ship in runtime-1.19 behind feature flag, default off.

[20:10] Connor O'Brien: Yes.

[20:12] Talia Benson: Decision 2: stage 1 perf-canary A/B required before prod canary. Run 48-72 hours.

[20:18] Jonas Weber: Yes.

[20:19] Talia Benson: Decision 3: stage 2 limited Dedicated slice with staffed on-call; requires SRE signoff with explicit rollback triggers.

[20:27] Sean Gallagher: Yes.

[20:28] Talia Benson: Action items: Rina reruns combined fixes; Omar publishes metric naming; Aisha finalizes alerts; Peter validates overload defaults; Sahana adds CI fairness gate; Connor confirms release inclusion; Sana drafts go/no-go criteria template.

[20:48] Sana Farid: Yep.

[20:50] Rina Kobayashi: I’ll try to get the reruns by Monday. If harness queue is clear.

[20:56] Jonas Weber: Ping me if you need more canary capacity.

[21:00] Sean Gallagher: And please send the rollback doc. I want it in the runbook with “if X then flip flag off.”

[21:07] Tomáš Novák: I can help write the runbook section.

[21:10] Talia Benson: Great. We’ll follow up in Linear with the checklist.

[21:15] (audio skips)

[21:18] Talia Benson: Anything else urgent?

[21:21] Rafael Mendes: Just one note: during canary, ensure we page the right rotation and not the whole company. Make a temporary alert route.

[21:28] Aisha Bello: Yes, I’ll set alert routing to the canary on-call channel.

[21:33] Talia Benson: Cool. Thanks all.

---

(Transcript continues with brief off-topic scheduling discussion; removed by Fireflies summarizer.)
